title: Hubble 1929: The Linear Distance–Velocity Relation as a First Approximation
concept_summary: Hubble's 1929 paper reports a linear correlation between distances and radial velocities of extra-galactic nebulae. The observed radial velocity v is modeled as a distance term plus three solar-motion terms; after removing the solar-motion terms, the simplified relation is v_corrected = d*K, where d is distance in Mpc and K is a historical slope in km/s per Mpc. The paper's fitted coefficients were 465 and 513, and it used the rounded value K=500. This lesson lets you sweep distance and slope to see the exact mean line, while stressing that real nebulae scatter about it and that the paper itself called the relation a first approximation over a restricted distance range.
why_it_matters: This is the classic observational statement that galaxy recession velocity grows roughly with distance. It matters because it links a measurable spectrum shift to a distance estimate, giving a quantitative handle on cosmic expansion. It also teaches a key modeling habit: a clean linear law can be a useful first approximation whose residuals, selection effects, and limited range must be examined before drawing stronger conclusions.

explanation_steps.heading: From observed velocity to a corrected distance term
explanation_steps.body: Hubble's equations of condition write the observed radial velocity as a distance term plus three terms describing the Sun's motion projected on the sky. The angular terms are removed to isolate the distance-dependent part, leaving the simplified teaching form v_corrected = d*K. Here d is distance in Mpc and K is the slope in km/s per Mpc.

explanation_steps.heading: The historical slope is a rounded value
explanation_steps.body: The paper reports fitted coefficients of 465 and 513 km/s per million parsecs and then adopts the rounded intermediate value K=500. That number is a historical teaching value from 1929, not a present-day measurement of the Hubble constant. Changing K changes the predicted velocity at every distance.

explanation_steps.heading: A first approximation with scatter
explanation_steps.body: The plotted corrected velocities still contain residuals, and the paper describes the linear relation as a first approximation over a restricted distance range. The exact line shown here is a simplified mean relation, not a fit to or reproduction of the observed nebular velocities. Real galaxies have peculiar motions, so not every point lies on the line.

visualizations.title: Simplified mean line: corrected velocity versus distance

explorations.change: Keep K at 500 and move the distance slider from 2 Mpc to 4 Mpc.
explorations.observe: The predicted velocity doubles from 1000 km/s to 2000 km/s, and the ratio computation stays at 2.
explorations.why: At fixed K the relation is linear through the origin, so doubling distance doubles the predicted corrected velocity. This is the proportionality the paper's linear correlation suggests.

explorations.change: Set distance to 2 Mpc and raise K from 500 to 600.
explorations.observe: The predicted velocity rises from 1000 km/s to 1200 km/s, and the line view becomes steeper.
explorations.why: K is the slope of the line, so increasing K increases the predicted velocity at every fixed distance. The paper's fitted values 465 and 513 bracket the rounded 500, showing the slope was uncertain.

limitations: The exact line v = K*d is a simplified mean relation after solar-motion correction, not a fit to or reproduction of observed nebular velocities.
Real nebulae have peculiar motions and residuals, so individual galaxies scatter about the line.
The paper describes the linear relation as a first approximation over a restricted distance range; it should not be extrapolated relativistically.
K=500 is the paper's rounded historical teaching value, not a present-day measurement of the Hubble constant.
This lesson does not infer the age of the universe or claim the source established an exact modern cosmology.
The solar-motion terms are not modeled numerically here; only their removal is represented by the simplified form.
